Scotland's Most Scenic Motorcycle Roads

Scotland contains some of the finest motorcycle roads in Europe. From dramatic mountain passes to remote single-track roads hugging the Atlantic coastline, the variety and intensity of Scottish riding is extraordinary. Here are the roads every motorcyclist should ride at least once.

A82 Through Glencoe

The A82 from Tyndrum to Fort William via Glencoe is Britain's most dramatic road. The pass itself rises between towering mountains — Buachaille Etive Mòr and the Three Sisters — creating a corridor of rock, water, and sky that feels almost otherworldly.

  • Distance: 32 miles (Tyndrum to Fort William)
  • Surface: Good tarmac, single carriageway with passing opportunities
  • Highlights: Rannoch Moor, Buachaille Etive Mòr, the Three Sisters, Loch Leven
  • Best time: Early morning for empty roads and dramatic light
  • Watch out for: Tourist traffic in summer, rain making the road surface slippery near the pass summit

Bealach na Bà (Applecross Pass)

The Bealach na Bà is Britain's answer to the Alpine passes. Rising from sea level to 2,054ft in just a few miles, it features hairpin bends, vertiginous drops, and views across to Skye and Raasay that stop you in your tracks.

  • Distance: 11 miles from the junction to Applecross village
  • Surface: Single-track with passing places. Good surface but narrow.
  • Gradient: Up to 20% — steep enough to require careful gear selection
  • Highlights: The hairpins, the summit viewpoint, the descent to Applecross with Skye panorama
  • Watch out for: Campervans and tourist traffic in summer. The road is closed in severe winter weather.

A87 to the Isle of Skye

The A87 from Invergarry to Kyle of Lochalsh crosses some of the most spectacular landscapes in Scotland. The road passes through Glen Shiel, where mountains rise steeply on both sides, and crosses the iconic Skye Bridge.

  • Distance: 55 miles
  • Highlights: Glen Shiel, the Five Sisters of Kintail, Eilean Donan Castle, Skye Bridge

NC500 (North Coast 500)

Scotland's answer to Route 66. A 500-mile loop from Inverness around the north coast, taking in the wildest, most remote, and most beautiful landscapes in Britain.

  • Distance: 516 miles (full loop)
  • Duration: 5-7 days recommended
  • Highlights: Bealach na Bà, Durness, Smoo Cave, Duncansby Head, Dunnet Head, Assynt
  • Surface: Mix of single-track, A-roads, and B-roads. Some sections are rough.

A838 / A894 Durness to Lairg via Loch Shin

This cross-Highland route cuts through some of the emptiest landscape in Britain. Pass by nothing but mountains, lochs, and the occasional red deer for mile after mile.

A85 Through Glen Ogle

Known as Scotland's Khyber Pass, the A85 through Glen Ogle is a dramatic climb through a narrow, steep-sided glen. The old railway viaduct visible from the road adds to the atmosphere.

B862 / B852 South Loch Ness Road

While everyone drives the A82 on the north side of Loch Ness, the south shore road (B862/B852) is the motorcyclist's choice. Narrower, twistier, and with better views of the loch, it's a hidden gem that most tourists miss entirely.

Scotland rewards the rider who goes beyond the obvious routes. The B-roads and single-track roads are where the real magic lives. Don't rush between the famous spots — the roads connecting them are often the best part.

Planning Tips for Scottish Roads

  • Fuel stations are sparse — never pass one below half tank
  • Single-track road etiquette: pull into passing places on your left to let oncoming traffic through
  • Sheep, deer, and cattle are genuine road hazards. Reduce speed near livestock.
  • Weather changes rapidly — be prepared for sun, rain, and mist in the same hour
  • Midges are brutal June-September. Carry repellent and a head net for stops.

Scotland's roads are the jewel in the British touring crown. Ride them with respect, patience, and open eyes, and you'll understand why riders return year after year. Read our Cairngorms Scenic Motorcycle Roads: Scotland's Mountain Heart guide for more.
keyTakeaways: The A82 through Glencoe and the Bealach na Ba (Applecross Pass) are Scotland's two must-ride roads, the latter climbing to 2,054ft on Alpine-style hairpins.
The NC500 is a 516-mile loop from Inverness best given 5 to 7 days rather than rushed.
The B862/B852 south Loch Ness road is far twistier and quieter than the tourist-heavy A82 north shore.
Fuel is sparse in the Highlands, so never pass a station below half a tank.
Ride early morning for empty roads and dramatic light, and carry midge repellent for stops between June and September.

faq.q: Is the Bealach na Ba suitable for a nervous or new rider?
faq.a: The Bealach na Ba is a single-track road with tight hairpins, gradients up to 20%, and steep drops, so it rewards confidence with the clutch and hill starts. Nervous riders should tackle it on a dry weekday morning before the campervans arrive. If it feels beyond you, the coast road via Shieldaig into Applecross is gentler and just as scenic.

faq.q: How long should I allow for the NC500?
faq.a: Five to seven days lets you actually enjoy the NC500 rather than just tick it off. The full loop is 516 miles, but the single-track sections, photo stops, and weather mean progress is slower than the mileage suggests. Rushing it in two or three days turns a world-class route into an endurance test and you will miss Durness, Assynt, and the best viewpoints.

faq.q: When is the best time of year to ride Scotland's roads?
faq.a: May and September are the sweet spots: long daylight, quieter roads, and far fewer midges than high summer. June to August brings the most reliable weather but also tourist traffic and brutal midges at stops. Winter closes some passes and brings ice, so it suits only well-prepared riders on clear, dry days.

faq.q: What are the main hazards on Highland single-track roads?
faq.a: Sheep, deer, and cattle wander onto the tarmac without warning, so reduce speed near livestock. Passing places are for letting oncoming traffic through and for allowing faster vehicles to overtake, not for parking. Loose gravel gathers on the crown and edges of remote roads, and the weather can change from sun to mist within a single hour.

faq.q: Where can I get the best photographs on these routes?
faq.a: The lay-by beneath Buachaille Etive Mor on the A82 is the classic Glencoe shot, and the summit of the Bealach na Ba looks back down the hairpins to the sea. Eilean Donan Castle on the A87 and the Rest and Be Thankful viewpoint are reliable stops. Aim for golden hour, first or last light, and place your bike in the foreground for scale.
